Only the two **quarter arcs** contribute; the straight sections pass through O and give
nothing.
**Step 1 — dispose of the straight parts.** For a straight segment, the Biot-Savart
element I d̄l̄ x r̂ vanishes when d̄l̄ is **along** r̂ ✓ The straight portions lie along
lines through O, so they contribute **zero**.
**Step 2 — find the field of one quarter arc.** A **full** circle of radius R gives
µ₀I/(2R) at its centre, so a quarter of it gives
B = (1/4)(µ₀I/2R) = **µ₀I/(8R)** ✓
**Step 3 — add the two arcs.** Both carry the same current and both send their field
the same way through O:
B = µ₀I/(8R₁) + µ₀I/(8R₂)
= (µ₀I/8)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂) ✓
**Step 4 — combine the fractions.**
= **(µ₀I/8)[(R₁ + R₂)/(R₁R₂)]** ✓
**Why the arcs add rather than cancel.** Tracing the current round the loop, both arcs
circulate in the **same rotational sense** about O ✓ so by the right-hand rule both
fields point the same way - out of the page or into it - and the magnitudes add.
**Why the smaller arc contributes more.** B ∝ 1/R ✓ so if R₁ is the smaller radius it
dominates. In the limit R₂ → ∞ the outer arc contributes nothing and the answer reduces
to µ₀I/(8R₁) - a useful check the formula passes.
**The general rule for an arc.** An arc subtending angle θ at the centre gives
B = **µ₀Iθ/(4πR)** ✓
For θ = π/2 this is µ₀I/(8R) ✓ and for θ = 2π it recovers µ₀I/(2R).
**A worked instance.** R₁ = 2 cm, R₂ = 4 cm, I = 10 A:
B = (4π x 10⁻⁷ x 10/8)(0·06/0·0008)
= (1·57 x 10⁻⁶)(75)
= **1·18 x 10⁻⁴ T** ✓
**Why the straight sections truly give nothing.** Each lies **radially**, so the angle
between d̄l̄ and r̂ is 0 or 180° and sin θ = 0 ✓ This is why such composite loops are
built from radial straights and concentric arcs - the geometry isolates the arcs'
contributions.
**Reading the distractors.** The option with **R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂)** ✗ is the reciprocal
combination - it would follow from adding the **radii's** reciprocals the wrong way
round. **Zero** ✗ would need the arcs to oppose, and the option with **R₁ − R₂** ✗
would need the current to circulate oppositely in the two ✓
∴ (µ₀I/8)[(R₁ + R₂)/(R₁R₂)].

The red light of a ruby laser comes from **chromium** ions.
**Step 1 — identify the material.** Ruby is **aluminium oxide**, Al₂O₃ - sapphire -
doped with about **0·05%** of **chromium** ✓ Pure Al₂O₃ is colourless; the chromium
gives both the stone's red colour and the laser's.
**Step 2 — identify the active species.** The **Cr³⁺ ions**, which replace a few of the
aluminium ions in the crystal lattice ✓ They absorb in the green and blue, and emit in
the deep red.
**Step 3 — note the wavelength.** **694·3 nm** ✓ the characteristic deep red of the
ruby laser.
**How the laser works.** A **flash lamp** - usually **xenon** - pumps the chromium ions
to higher levels ✓ They decay rapidly to a **metastable** level with a lifetime of
about **3 ms**, long enough for a population inversion to build. Stimulated emission
then dumps the energy as an intense red pulse.
**Why xenon is a distractor.** The xenon flash lamp is the **pump**, not the source of
the light ✓ Its own emission is broadband white; the red colour comes entirely from the
chromium.
**Why aluminium is a distractor.** It is the **host** lattice ✓ Al₂O₃ is transparent
and plays no part in the emission - it merely holds the chromium ions in place and
conducts away the heat.
**The historical importance.** Theodore Maiman built the **first working laser** from a
ruby rod in **1960** ✓ It was a three-level system and could only be pulsed, but it
opened the field.
**Why a three-level laser must be pulsed.** The lower laser level is the **ground
state**, which is heavily populated ✓ More than half the ions must be pumped up before
inversion is achieved - which demands an enormous flash. Four-level lasers such as
Nd:YAG empty their lower level automatically and can run continuously.
**Why ruby is red at all.** The same Cr³⁺ absorption in the green and violet ✓ so the
transmitted light is red. Replace the chromium with iron and titanium and the same
crystal becomes blue sapphire.
**Reading the distractors.** **Aluminium** ✗ is the host, **xenon** ✗ the pump, and
**oxygen** ✗ merely part of the lattice ✓ Only chromium undergoes the lasing
transition.
∴ Chromium.

Light escapes only within the **critical cone**, so the patch has radius **h tan C**.
**Step 1 — find the critical angle.**
sin C = 1/n
= 1/(4/3)
= **3/4** ✓
**Step 2 — find its tangent.** With sin C = 3/4, the right triangle has opposite 3,
hypotenuse 4 and adjacent **√7**:
**tan C = 3/√7** ✓
**Step 3 — find the radius of the patch.**
r = h tan C
= √7 x (3/√7)
= **3 m** ✓
**Why only a circular patch is lit.** Rays leaving the source at angles **beyond** C
are **totally internally reflected** at the surface and never escape ✓ Only those
within the cone of half-angle C emerge, and they strike the surface inside a circle of
radius h tan C.
**Why the depth is chosen as √7.** It cancels the √7 in tan C exactly ✓ giving the
clean answer 3 m. Examiners pick such values deliberately.
**The critical angle's value.** C = sin⁻¹(0·75) = **48·6°** ✓ so the escape cone is
nearly 97° wide in total.
**What an observer above sees.** A bright circular patch of radius 3 m, beyond which
the surface looks **silvered** ✓ reflecting the pond bottom rather than transmitting
the source's light.
**The companion effect - Snell's window.** Looking **up** from under water, a diver
sees the entire sky compressed into a circle of half-angle **48·6°** ✓ the same cone,
traversed in the opposite direction.
**Why the radius scales with depth.** r = h tan C ✓ so a source twice as deep lights a
patch twice as wide, and the **area** quadruples. The fraction of light escaping,
however, stays the same.
**How much light actually escapes.** The solid angle of the cone is
2π(1 − cos C) = 2π(1 − 0·661) = **2·13 sr** out of 4π ✓ about **17%** - which is why
underwater lights seem so dim from above.
**A worked check.** A ray at exactly 48·6° from the vertical travels
√7/cos(48·6°) = **4 m** to the surface, arriving 3 m from the point directly above ✓
consistent with the 3-√7-4 triangle.
**Reading the distractors.** **√7** ✗ is the depth itself, **√7/3** ✗ and **3/√7** ✗
are the tangent and its reciprocal read as lengths ✓
∴ 3.

Three resistors in **parallel** share the current in proportion to their
**conductances**.
**Step 1 — write the conductances.** In parallel the voltage is common, so I ∝ 1/R:
1/10, 1/15, 1/20 ✓
**Step 2 — put them over a common denominator of 60.**
6/60, 4/60, 3/60 ✓
total = **13/60**
**Step 3 — find the share taken by the 15 Ω branch.**
I₂ = 1·2 x (4/13)
= 4·8/13
= **0·369 ≈ 0·4 A** ✓
**Step 4 — check the other two.**
I₁ = 1·2(6/13) = **0·554 A**
I₃ = 1·2(3/13) = **0·277 A** ✓
total 0·554 + 0·369 + 0·277 = **1·2 A** ✓ as it must be.
**Why the smallest resistance takes the most.** It offers the easiest path ✓ The
currents are in the ratio 6 : 4 : 3, exactly the inverse of 10 : 15 : 20.
**The equivalent resistance.**
1/R = 13/60, so **R = 4·62 Ω** ✓ less than the smallest branch, as a parallel
combination must be.
**The common voltage.**
V = IR = 1·2 x 4·62 = **5·54 V** ✓
and a check: 5·54/15 = **0·369 A** ✓ exactly I₂.
**The current-divider rule for several branches.**
**I_k = I x (1/R_k)/Σ(1/R)** ✓
The branch's **own** conductance in the numerator, the total in the denominator.
**Why the three-branch case needs care.** With only two branches the familiar
I₁ = I R₂/(R₁ + R₂) works ✓ but with three it is simpler and safer to use
conductances, as above - the two-branch shortcut does not generalise.
**How the power divides.** P = V²/R, so also in the ratio 6 : 4 : 3 ✓ The 10 Ω
dissipates 3·07 W, the 15 Ω 2·05 W and the 20 Ω 1·53 W, totalling 6·65 W - which equals
1·2 x 5·54 ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **0·6 A** ✗ is closer to I₁. **0·3 A** ✗ is near I₃, and
**0·2 A** ✗ smaller still ✓ Checking that the three currents sum to 1·2 A identifies
the right one at once.
∴ 0.4 A.

Sunlight is a **continuous** spectrum crossed by dark **Fraunhofer** lines - a **line
absorption** spectrum.
**Step 1 — identify the continuous source.** The Sun's **photosphere** is hot and
dense, radiating approximately as a black body at **5800 K** ✓ That alone would give a
smooth continuum.
**Step 2 — identify the absorber.** The cooler gases of the **chromosphere** lie above
it ✓ Each element absorbs at exactly the wavelengths it would emit, cutting narrow
dark slices from the continuum.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Dark lines on a bright background - a **line absorption**
spectrum ✓
**The Fraunhofer lines.** Catalogued in 1814 and labelled A, B, C, D… ✓
**D lines** at 589 nm: **sodium**
**H and K**: **calcium**
**C and F**: hydrogen's H_α and H_β ✓
Over 25000 are now known.
**Why the lines are dark but not black.** The absorbing layer **re-emits** the energy -
but in all directions ✓ so only a fraction continues towards us and the line appears
dim rather than empty.
**What the lines reveal.** The Sun's **composition**, element by element ✓ This is how
we know it is 71% hydrogen and 27% helium - and how **helium** itself was discovered
in 1868, before being found on Earth.
**Kirchhoff's law behind it.** A gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths it emits ✓ Seen
**against** the photosphere the chromosphere's lines are **dark**; seen against the
dark sky during a total eclipse, the very same lines flash **bright**.
**What else spectra tell us.** **Doppler shifts** give radial velocities - revealing
binary stars, exoplanets and the expansion of the universe ✓ **Zeeman splitting**
measures magnetic fields, and line **widths** give temperatures and pressures.
**Why not "continuous emission".** That describes the photosphere **alone** ✓ but what
reaches us has been filtered, and the lines are the most informative part of the
spectrum.
**Reading the distractors.** **Continuous emission** ✗ ignores the lines.
**Continuous absorption** ✗ would mean broad regions removed, as a coloured filter
does. **Band emission** ✗ needs molecules, and would be emission rather than
absorption ✓
∴ Line absorption spectrum.

Form the ratio of the two exponentials; the common N₀ cancels.
**Step 1 — write each survival.**
N_A = N₀e^(−15xt)
N_B = N₀e^(−3xt) ✓
**Step 2 — take the ratio.**
N_A/N_B = e^(−15xt)/e^(−3xt)
= **e^(−12xt)** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute t = 1/(6x).**
−12x x 1/(6x) = **−2** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.**
N_A/N_B = **e⁻²** ✓
**Why A is so far behind.** Its decay constant is **five times** B's, so it decays five
times faster ✓ After the stated interval only e⁻² = **13·5%** as many A nuclei survive
as B nuclei.
**The absolute survivals, for scale.**
N_A/N₀ = e^(−15/6) = e^(−2·5) = **8·2%**
N_B/N₀ = e^(−3/6) = e^(−0·5) = **60·7%** ✓
and the ratio 8·2/60·7 = **0·135 = e⁻²** ✓ confirming the result.
**The two half-lives.**
T_A = 0·693/15x = **0·0462/x**
T_B = 0·693/3x = **0·231/x** ✓
so B lives five times as long, and the elapsed time 1/(6x) = 0·167/x is about 3·6
half-lives for A but only 0·72 for B.
**Why the initial numbers cancel.** They are **equal**, and both appear as N₀ ✓ Only
the exponents matter, which is what makes the ratio so clean.
**Why the decay constant, not the half-life, is the natural parameter.** λ is the
**probability per unit time** that any given nucleus decays ✓ It appears directly in
the exponential, whereas the half-life carries the awkward ln 2.
**The memoryless property behind it all.** Every surviving nucleus has the **same**
chance of decaying next, regardless of how long it has existed ✓ That constant hazard
is exactly what produces an exponential.
**A caution on the sign.** The ratio is **less** than 1, since A decays faster ✓ An
answer of e² or e would mean A outlasting B - impossible with the larger decay
constant.
**Reading the distractors.** **e²** ✗ and **e** ✗ are both greater than 1. **e⁻¹** ✗
would need an exponent of −6xt, that is a difference of 6x rather than 12x ✓
∴ e⁻².

The **proton** is the only stable baryon.
**Step 1 — recall what a baryon is.** A hadron built from **three quarks** ✓ The proton
(uud) and the neutron (udd) are the lightest; the lambda, sigma, xi and omega are
heavier.
**Step 2 — compare the lifetimes.**
**proton**: no decay ever observed ✓ experiment sets a lower limit above **10³⁴ years**
**neutron**: free, a half-life of about **10·2 minutes** ✓
**lambda**: **2·6 x 10⁻¹⁰ s** ✓
**sigma**: 10⁻¹⁰ s or less
**Step 3 — conclude.** The **proton** ✓ - stable so far as any experiment can tell.
**Why the proton cannot decay.** It is the **lightest** baryon ✓ and **baryon number**
is conserved in every observed interaction, so there is no lighter baryon for it to
become. Conservation of energy and of baryon number together protect it absolutely.
**Why the neutron can.** It is **heavier** than the proton by 1·3 MeV, so
n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ is energetically allowed ✓ and the weak interaction permits it.
**Why neutrons survive inside nuclei.** The binding energy makes the decay
energetically **forbidden** in a stable nucleus ✓ which is why ordinary matter endures
although free neutrons do not.
**Why the heavier baryons go so fast.** They contain **strange** quarks and decay by
the strong or weak interaction into lighter states ✓ Nothing conserves strangeness in
weak decays, so they have ample channels open.
**Why physicists hunt for proton decay.** Grand unified theories predict a lifetime of
10³¹ to 10³⁶ years ✓ **Super-Kamiokande** has watched 50000 tonnes of water for
decades and seen nothing, ruling out the simplest such theories.
**Why the proton's stability matters.** All ordinary matter rests on it ✓ If it decayed
appreciably, atoms, stars and we ourselves would dissolve. Its stability is among the
most important facts in physics.
**The classification, for context.**
**baryons**: three quarks ✓
**mesons**: quark-antiquark - pion, kaon ✓
**leptons**: fundamental, no quarks - electron, neutrinos ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Neutron** ✗ lives only minutes when free. **Lambda** and
**sigma** ✗ decay in fractions of a nanosecond ✓
∴ Proton.
